summary: Describes mechanisms that improve SigComp compression efficiency compared with compressing each message on its own, such as using state saved from earlier messages. They are built using the instructions of the SigComp Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine. It was later updated by RFC 4896.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3321 describes ways for SigComp to reuse information from earlier messages and improve compression. A sender can use a saved state only after it knows the receiver has that state.

subtitle: Optional SigComp mechanisms for reusing message data and confirming saved compression state.

tldr.problem: Compressing every message independently wastes bandwidth, while reusing earlier data requires confidence that the receiver has saved the same state.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes acknowledgements, shared compression, cross-session state, user-specific dictionaries, checkpoint states, and implicit dictionary deletion using existing UDVM instructions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3321 is an Informational memo, not an Internet Standard, and was updated by RFC 4896. It builds on RFC 3320.

today: RFC 3321 describes itself as Informational and says it does not specify an Internet Standard. It was updated by RFC 4896 and builds on RFC 3320.

sections.title: Beyond Independent Message Compression
sections.content:
SigComp can compress each message independently, but later messages may repeat information already sent. This RFC describes dynamic compression, which reuses earlier sent messages, and shared compression, which reuses messages received by the local endpoint.

On a reliable transport such as TCP, the sender knows earlier messages arrived. On an unreliable transport, explicit acknowledgement lets the receiver confirm that it saved a state. The mechanisms use UDVM instructions defined by RFC 3320 and do not require new instructions.
sections.plainLanguage: Later messages often repeat information from earlier messages. SigComp can reuse that information to compress more effectively, but must know what the receiver has saved.

sections.title: Saved and Acknowledged States
sections.content:
A state is saved UDVM memory that a later message can reference by a state identifier. A saved state is intended for later use; an acknowledged state is one the compressor knows the remote decompressor established.

A compressor must use only acknowledged states for dynamic compression. Otherwise, a lost message could leave the receiver without the state required to decompress a later message.

Acknowledgements travel in SigComp feedback, normally on messages in the opposite direction. The RFC's example shows how a sender can keep using confirmed state after an unacknowledged message is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender must not rely on a state until the receiver confirms it saved that state. This prevents a later message from depending on information the receiver does not have.

sections.title: Explicit Acknowledgement
sections.content:
When messages may be lost or reordered, the remote compressor needs an acknowledgement that a state exists at the decompressor. The RFC describes two approaches.

In remote-compressor initiation, the sender places a requested-feedback identifier in the compressed message, and the receiver returns it in feedback. The identifier should be at least one octet and long enough to avoid acknowledging the wrong state.

In local-endpoint initiation, the endpoint that saved the state sends its state identifier back in the returned parameters. The RFC says not to use this approach when requested feedback is nonzero because it can waste bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: Feedback can confirm that the receiver saved a state. The sender then knows it can safely use that state in later compression.

sections.title: Shared Compression
sections.content:
Shared compression saves the uncompressed version of a message as a state. Because this shared state contains the message itself, it is independent of the compression algorithm used in either direction.

The receiver calculates a shared-state identifier with the SHA-1 instruction and returns it in SigComp parameters. The sender can use the shared state after it confirms that the receiver retained the same state.

Shared states consume the same state memory as other states. A compressor must make enough memory available before creating one, or it could displace state that the receiver needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint can save the uncompressed message it received and refer to it later. Both ends compare its identifier before using it for compression.

sections.title: Other State-Efficiency Methods
sections.content:
The RFC describes several related techniques. A compartment can keep state across application sessions, and a compressor can send a user-specific dictionary before time-critical messages begin.

A checkpoint state uses the highest retention priority sent by a compressor and must be explicitly acknowledged. This helps avoid references to states that were never saved or were later removed for lack of memory.

With implicit deletion, both endpoints apply the same defined algorithm to remove dictionary data. This avoids signaling the deletion choice in each message.
sections.plainLanguage: SigComp can retain state across sessions, send a dictionary early, and protect important states from removal. Both endpoints can also use the same rule to delete dictionary data.

sections.title: Information Carried in SigComp Messages
sections.content:
Extended operations may need an acknowledged-state identifier or a shared-state identifier in a SigComp message. The RFC leaves the format after the mandatory message bytes to the implementation and compressor bytecode.

A basic SigComp implementation ignores the extra identifiers and is not affected by receiving them. An endpoint that wants shared-state identifiers must not set the I-bit of the requested feedback format to one.
sections.plainLanguage: Extended features can add state identifiers to SigComp messages. Implementations that do not use these features can ignore those identifiers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the described features are believed not to add security risks beyond those already described for SigComp in RFC 3320. It requires no IANA action.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says these features do not add known security risks beyond those in basic SigComp. It requests no IANA action.
